I have pointed this out so that one is not deceived by much of what a group of the exegetes mentioned at this verse, namely the mention of a city called ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾, built with bricks of gold and silver, whose palaces, houses, and gardens, whose pebbles are pearls and jewels, whose dust is musk pellets, whose rivers flow, whose fruits are abundant, whose houses have no inhabitant, whose walls and doors turn yellow, with no caller and no answerer in it, and which moves: at times it is in the land of Syria, at times in Yemen, at times in Iraq, and at times in other lands. All of this is from the fabrications of the Israelites, put forward by some of their heretics, to test with it the intellects of ignorant people, to see whether they will believe them in all of it.

Al-Tha'labi and others mentioned that a man from the Bedouins, who was ʿAbd Allah ibn Qilabah, in the time of Muʿawiyah, went in search of camels of his that had strayed. While he was wandering in searching for them, he came upon a great city with a wall and gates. He entered it and found in it something similar to what we have mentioned of the qualities of the golden city mentioned earlier. He returned and informed the people, and they went with him to the place he described, but they saw nothing.

Ibn Abi Hatim has mentioned the story of ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ here at great length, but this narration does not have a sound chain of transmission. Even if it were sound up to that Bedouin, he may have fabricated it, or some kind of madness and delusion afflicted him, so he believed that this had real existence outside the mind, when it does not. This is among matters whose unsoundness is certain. This is similar to what many ignorant, greedy, and deceptive people report, about the existence of treasures beneath the earth containing heaps of gold and silver, colors of jewels, rubies, pearls, and the great elixir, but there are barriers preventing access to them and taking from them. They then scheme against the wealth of the rich, the weak, and the foolish, consuming it wrongfully by spending it on incense, herbal remedies, and similar nonsense, and they mock them. What is certain is that the earth contains ancient treasures from the pre-Islamic and Islamic periods, and many hoards; whoever obtains some of them is able to transform them. But as for them being in the manner they claim, it is a lie, a fabrication, and a slander, and nothing of what they say is established except through their own transmission or the transmission of those who took from them. God, glory be to Him and exalted, is the Guide to what is right.

Ibn Jarir's statement: "It is possible that the meaning of His saying, ﴿Iram﴾, is a tribe or a town where ʿĀd used to dwell, and therefore it is not declined (lam tusraf)" has a problem with it, because the meaning from the context is only to inform about the tribe. For this reason He said after it: ﴿And Thamud, who carved out the rock in the valley﴾, meaning: they cut the rock in the valley. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they hewed it and cut through it. Likewise said Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd. From this one says "mujtabi al-nimar", meaning those who cut through the striped cloth, and ijtaba al-thawb means when he opened it. From it also comes the "jayb" (the opening of a garment). God, exalted, said: ﴿And you carve houses out of the mountains, skillfully﴾ [Al-Shuʿara': 149]. Here Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recited the verse of the poet:

Surely everything, except God, is perishing,
just as a tribe of Shanif and Marid perished.
They struck in every solid rock a hewing
with strong hands, sinewy of forearm.

[Tafsir al-Tabari (30/113).]

Ibn Ishaq said: They were Arabs, and their dwelling was in Wadi al-Qura. We have mentioned the story of ʿĀd in full in Surah Al-A'raf, sufficiently so that it need not be repeated.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿and Pharaoh, owner of the stakes﴾: al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: the stakes are the soldiers who strengthened his command. It is said that Pharaoh would fasten their hands and feet to stakes of iron, hanging them by them. Likewise Mujahid said: He used to fasten people to stakes. Thus said Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi. Al-Suddi said: He would tie a man, each of his limbs to a stake, and then send upon him a great boulder which would crush him.

Qatadah said: It has reached us that he had platforms and places of amusement, under which he would play, made of stakes and ropes.

Thabit al-Bunani said, from Abu Rafi': Pharaoh was called ﴿owner of the stakes﴾ because he drove four stakes for his wife, then placed upon her back a great millstone until she died.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿who transgressed in the lands and multiplied corruption therein﴾, meaning: they rebelled, became overbearing, and spread corruption in the earth through causing mischief and harm to people. ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a whip of punishment﴾, meaning: He sent down upon them a scourge from the sky and brought upon them a punishment that cannot be repelled from the criminal people.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: He hears and sees, meaning: He watches His creation in what they do, and recompenses each for his striving in this world and the Hereafter. All creatures will be presented before Him, and He will judge among them with His justice, and will deal with each according to what he deserves. He is free from injustice and oppression.

Ibn Abi Hatim has narrated here a very strange hadith, and its chain is questionable as to its soundness. He said: My father narrated to us, Ahmad ibn Abi al-Hawari narrated to us, Yunus al-Haddha' narrated to us, from Abu Hamza al-Baysani, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Mu'adh, verily the believer is a captive to the truth. O Mu'adh, verily the believer's fear does not subside and his agitation is not secure until he leaves the Bridge of Hell behind his back. O Mu'adh, verily the Qur'an restrains the believer from many of his desires, and from perishing in them, by the permission of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So the Qur'an is his guide, fear is his path, longing is his mount, prayer is his shelter, fasting is his shield, charity is his ransom, truthfulness is his commander, modesty is his minister, and his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is watching over all of that from behind [him]." [[Abu Nu'aym narrated it in al-Hilya (10/31) by way of Ishaq ibn Abi Hassan, from Ahmad ibn Abi al-Hawari with the same wording. Abu Nu'aym also narrated it in al-Hilya (1/26) by way of Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Karima, from Abu Hajib, from Abd al-Rahman, from Mu'adh, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) in similar wording.]].

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Yunus al-Haddha' and Abu Hamza are both unknown narrators (majhul, meaning their reliability is not established), and Abu Hamza's narration from Mu'adh is mursal (a break in the chain, where the Companion's name is missing). Had it been from Abu Hamza, it would have been good; that is, had it been from his own speech (not attributed to the Prophet), it would have been good.

Then Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Safwan ibn Salih narrated to us, al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, from Safwan ibn Amr, from Ayfa' ibn Abd al-Kula'i, that he heard him while he was admonishing the people, saying: "Verily Hell has seven bridges," and he said: "And the Sirat is over them." He said: "So the creatures will be held at the first bridge, and it will be said: ﴿And stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat: 24]. He said: They will be held accountable for the prayer and questioned about it. He said: Whoever is to perish, perishes there, and whoever is to be saved, is saved. When they reach the second bridge, they will be called to account for trust (amanah): how they fulfilled it and how they betrayed it. He said: Whoever is to perish, perishes, and whoever is to be saved, is saved. When they reach the third bridge, they will be questioned about the ties of kinship: how they upheld them and how they severed them. He said: Whoever is to perish, perishes, and whoever is to be saved, is saved. He said: On that Day the ties of kinship will be hanging down into the abyss of Hell, saying: O Allah, whoever has upheld me, then unite him, and whoever has severed me, then sever him. He said: And it is this of which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾."

Thus did he cite this report, but he did not mention its complete text.

**Tafsir of Surah al-Fajr**

It is a Meccan surah.

Al-Nasa'i said: Abd al-Wahhab ibn al-Hakam informed us, Yahya ibn Sa'id informed me, from Sulayman, from Muharib ibn Dithar and Abu Salih, from Jabir, who said: Mu'adh led a prayer, and a man came and prayed with him, and he [Mu'adh] prolonged it. So the man prayed in a corner of the mosque and then left. When this reached Mu'adh, he said: "He is a hypocrite." This was mentioned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he asked the young man. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I came to pray with him, and he prolonged it for me, so I left, prayed in a corner of the mosque, and tethered my water-camel." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Are you causing trouble, O Mu'adh? Where are you in relation to ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [87:1], ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [91:1], ﴿By the dawn﴾ [89:1], ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ [92:1]?" [Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra, no. 11673.]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

* *

As for ﴿al-Fajr﴾ (the dawn), it is well known, and it is the Subh (morning prayer/dawn). This was said by Ali, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah and al-Suddi. It is also reported from Masruq, Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b that what is meant is specifically the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr), which is the conclusion of the ten nights.

It was also said that what is meant is the prayer performed at that time, as Ikrimah said.

It was said that what is meant is the whole day. This is a report from Ibn Abbas.

As for ﴿the ten nights﴾: what is meant by them is the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, as said by Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and many others of the early and later scholars. It is established in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "There are no days in which righteous deeds are more beloved to Allah than these days" — meaning the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. They said: "Not even jihad in the way of Allah?" He said: "Not even jihad in the way of Allah, except for a man who goes out with his self and his wealth and does not return with anything of that." [Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 969.]

It was also said that what is meant is the first ten nights of Muharram. Abu Ja'far Ibn Jarir reported this without attributing it to anyone. Abu Kudayna narrated from Qabus ibn Abi Zibyan, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿and ten nights﴾, that he said: "It is the first ten [nights] of Ramadan."

The correct view is the first one. Imam Ahmad said:

Zayd ibn al-Hubab narrated to us, Ayyash ibn Uqba narrated to us, Khayr ibn Nu'aym narrated to me, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed the ten are the ten of al-Adha (Sacrifice), the odd is the Day of Arafah, and the even is the Day of Sacrifice."

al-Nasa'i narrated it from Muhammad ibn Rafi' and Abdah ibn Abd Allah, each of them from Zayd ibn al-Hubab, with the same chain. [al-Musnad (3/327) and Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra, no. 11671.] Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it from the hadith of Zayd ibn al-Hubab, with the same chain. [Tafsir al-Tabari (30/108).] This is a chain whose narrators are acceptable (la ba's bihim), but in my view the wording of its marfu' (traced-to-the-Prophet) form contains a strangeness (nakarah). And Allah knows best.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿By the even and the odd﴾: it has already been mentioned in this hadith that the odd is the Day of Arafah, because it is the ninth, and the even is the Day of Sacrifice, because it is the tenth. This was also said by Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah and al-Dahhak.

A second view: Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj narrated to us, Uqba ibn Khalid narrated to me, from Wasil ibn al-Sa'ib, who said: I asked Ata about His saying ﴿By the even and the odd﴾. I said: "Is it our prayer, this odd (witr) of ours?" He said: "No, but the even is the Day of Arafah, and the odd is the night of the Sacrifice."

A third view: Ibn Abi Hatim said: Muhammad ibn Amir ibn Ibrahim al-Asbahani narrated to us, my father narrated to me, from al-Nu'man, meaning Ibn Abd al-Salam, from Abu Sa'id ibn Awf, who narrated to me in Mecca, saying: I heard Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr giving a sermon to the people. A man stood up to him and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, inform me about the even and the odd." He said: "The even is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾, and the odd is His saying: ﴿and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾" [al-Baqarah 2:203].

Ibn Jurayj said: Muhammad ibn al-Murtafi' informed me that he heard Ibn al-Zubayr say: "The even is the middle of the days of Tashriq, and the odd is the last of the days of Tashriq."

In the two Sahihs, from the narration of Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one. Whoever enumerates them enters Paradise, and He is Odd (witr) and loves the odd." [Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 6410; Sahih Muslim, no. 2677.]

A fourth view: al-Hasan al-Basri and Zayd ibn Aslam said: All of creation is even and odd; Allah swore by His creation. This is also a report from Mujahid, but the well-known view from him is the first.

al-Awfi narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿By the even and the odd﴾ that he said: "Allah is one odd, and you are even." It is also said: the even is the dawn prayer (Subh) and the odd is the sunset prayer (Maghrib).

A fifth view: Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj narrated to us, Ubayd ibn Musa narrated to us, from Isra'il, from Abu Yahya, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿By the even and the odd﴾: "The even is the pair, and the odd is Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Abu Abd Allah said, from Mujahid: "Allah is the Odd, and His creation is the Even: the male and the female."

Ibn Abi Najih said, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿By the even and the odd﴾: "Everything Allah created is even: the heaven and the earth, the land and the sea, the jinn and the humans, the sun and the moon, and the like." Mujahid went in this direction with what they mentioned regarding the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And of everything We created pairs, that you may remember﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:49], meaning: so that you know that the Creator of the pairs is One.

A sixth view: Qatadah said, from al-Hasan: ﴿By the even and the odd﴾ is the number; within it is the even and within it is the odd.

A seventh view: concerning the noble verse, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir narrated it through the route of Ibn Jurayj. Then Ibn Jarir said: It has also been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) a report that supports the view we mentioned from Abu al-Zubayr: al-Husayn? [sic] Abd Allah ibn Abi Ziyad al-Qatawani narrated to me, Zayd ibn al-Hubab narrated to us, Ayyash ibn Uqba informed me, Khayr ibn Nu'aym narrated to me, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The even is the two days, and the odd is the third day." [Tafsir al-Tabari (30/109).]

This report has come in exactly this wording, and it contradicts what preceded in the wording of the narrations of Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Abi Hatim, and what he [Ibn Jarir] himself narrated. And Allah knows best.

Abu al-Aliyah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others said: It is the prayer. Among it is the even, like the four-rak'ah and two-rak'ah prayers, and among it is the odd, like the Maghrib, which is three, and it is the odd of the day. Likewise the Witr prayer at the end of the night's tahajjud.

Abd al-Razzaq said, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, from Imran ibn Husayn: ﴿By the even and the odd﴾: "It is the obligatory prayer; among it is the even and among it is the odd." This is disconnected (munqati') and halted (mawquf), and its wording is specific to the obligatory prayer. But it has been narrated connected and traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), with a general wording. Imam Ahmad said:

Abu Dawud, meaning al-Tayalisi, narrated to us, Hammam narrated to us, from Qatadah, from Imran ibn Isam: that a shaykh from the people of Basra narrated to him, from Imran ibn Husayn, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about the even and the odd, and he said: "It is the prayer; some of it is even and some of it is odd." [al-Musnad (4/437).]

This is how it appears in the Musnad. Likewise Ibn Jarir narrated it from Bundar, from Affan, and from Abu Kurayb, from Ubayd Allah ibn Musa, both of them from Hammam, meaning Ibn Yahya, from Qatadah, from Imran ibn Isam, from a shaykh, from Imran ibn Husayn. [Tafsir al-Tabari (30/109).] Likewise Abu Isa al-Tirmidhi narrated it from Amr ibn Ali, from Ibn Mahdi and Abu Dawud, both of them from Hammam, from Qatadah, from Imran ibn Isam, from a man from the people of Basra, from Imran ibn Husayn, with it. Then he said: "Gharib (strange); we do not know it except from the hadith of Qatadah, and Khalid ibn Qays also narrated it from Qatadah." [Sunan al-Tirmidhi, no. 3342.]

It has also been narrated from Imran ibn Isam, from Imran himself. And Allah knows best.

I say: Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it: Ahmad ibn Sinan al-Wasiti narrated to us, Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, Hammam informed us, from Qatadah, from Imran ibn Isam al-Dubaʿi, a shaykh from the people of Basra, from Imran ibn Husayn, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he mentioned it. Thus I saw it in his tafsir, where he made the Basran shaykh to be Imran ibn Isam [al-Dubaʿi].

Likewise Ibn Jarir narrated it: Nasr ibn Ali narrated to us, my father narrated to me, Khalid ibn Qays narrated to me, from Qatadah, from Imran ibn Isam, from Imran ibn Husayn, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding the even and the odd, that he said: "It is the prayer; among it is the even, and among it is the odd." [Tafsir al-Tabari (30/109).]

So he [the narrator] omitted the mention of the unnamed shaykh, and Imran ibn Isam al-Dubaʿi, Abu Umarah al-Basri, the imam of the mosque of Banu Dubay'ah, was alone in narrating it. He is the father of Abu Jamrah Nasr ibn Imran al-Dubaʿi. Qatadah narrated from him, and his son Abu Jamrah, al-Muthanna ibn Sa'id and Abu al-Tayyah Yazid ibn Humayd. Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat (the Reliable Narrators) [al-Thiqat (5/234)], and Khalifah ibn Khayyat mentioned him among the Successors (al-Tabi'in) from the people of Basra. He was a noble, honored man, highly regarded by al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf. Then he was killed on the day of al-Zawiyah in the year eighty-three (in another copy: eighty-two), because he went out with Ibn al-Ash'ath. He has in al-Tirmidhi only this single hadith. In my view, its being halted (mawquf) upon Imran ibn Husayn is more likely. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Jarir did not decide definitively on any of these views regarding the even and the odd.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾ [yasri]: al-Awfi narrated from Ibn Abbas: "That is, when it goes away."

Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr said: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾, until some of it removes the others.

Mujahid, Abu al-Aliyah, Qatadah, Malik, from Zayd ibn Aslam, and Ibn Zayd said: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾: "when it travels."

This can be understood according to what Ibn Abbas said, that is, it departs. It may also be that what is meant is when it travels, that is, it approaches. It may be said that this is more fitting, because it is in contrast to His saying ﴿and the dawn﴾, for the dawn is the approach of day and the withdrawal of night. So when His saying ﴿And the night when it passes﴾ is understood as its approach, it becomes an oath by the approach of night and the withdrawal of day, and vice versa, like His saying: ﴿And the night when it withdraws, and the morning when it breathes﴾ [al-Takwir 81:17–18]. Likewise al-Dahhak said: ﴿[And the night] when it passes﴾: that is, it flows.

Ikrimah said: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾ means: the night of Jam' (Muzdalifah). Narrated by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim.

Then Ibn Abi Hatim said: Ahmad ibn Isam narrated to us, Abu Amir narrated to us, Kathir ibn Abd Allah ibn Amr narrated to us, who said: I heard Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi say regarding His saying ﴿And the night when it passes﴾: "Pass on, O traveler, and do not reveal yourself except at Jam'."

* *

And His saying: ﴿Is there in that an oath for one of intellect?﴾ meaning: for one who has reason, understanding, and restraint [and religion] [[addition from manuscript M.]]. Reason is called ḥijr because it restrains a person from engaging in deeds and words that are unbecoming to him. From the same root comes ḥijr al-Bayt (the Hijr of the Ka'bah), because it prevents the circumambulator from pressing against its Syrian wall. Also from it is Ḥijr al-Yamamah (the Hijr of Yamamah). When a judge places a man under restriction (ḥajara 'ala fulan), he prevents him from disposing of his property. ﴿And they say, "A forbidding forbidding"﴾ [Al-Furqan: 22]. All of these belong to one category and have closely related meanings. This oath is by the times of worship and by worship itself, such as pilgrimage, prayer, and other kinds of acts of drawing near to God, by which His servants draw near to Him, the God-fearing who obey Him, who fear Him, who are humble before Him, and who are submissive to His noble Countenance.

When He mentioned these people, their worship, and their obedience, He said after them: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd?﴾ These people were rebellious, stubborn, and tyrannical, who departed from His obedience, denied His messengers, and rejected His scriptures. So God mentioned how He destroyed and annihilated them, and made them into tales and lessons. He said: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd, Iram of the pillars?﴾ These were the first ʿĀd, the descendants of ʿĀd ibn Iram ibn ʿAws ibn Sam ibn Nuh, as Ibn Ishaq said. They are the people among whom God sent His messenger Hud, peace be upon him, but they denied him and opposed him. So God saved him from among them, along with those who believed with him, and destroyed them with a violent, furious wind, ﴿which He imposed upon them for seven nights and eight days in succession, so that you would see the people in it fallen as if they were trunks of hollow palm trees. Do you see any remnant of them?﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 7–8]. God has mentioned their story in the Qur'an in more than one place, so that believers may take warning from their downfall.

So His saying, ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ [[in M: "bi-ʿĀd Iram".]] is ʿatf al-bayan (explicative apposition, ʿaṭf al-bayān, a noun placed after another to clarify it), serving to give further identification of them.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿of the pillars﴾: they used to live in tents of hair that were raised upon strong pillars. They were also the strongest people of their time in physical build and the most powerful in their force. For this reason Hud reminded them of that blessing and guided them to use it in obedience to their Lord who created them. He said: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Nuh and increased you in stature and build. So remember the bounties of God that you may succeed﴾ [[in M, A, H: "and do not commit corruption on earth, causing mischief," and the correct reading is what we have adopted.]] [Al-A'raf: 69]. And He said: ﴿As for ʿĀd, they were arrogant upon the earth without right and said, "Who is stronger than us in strength?" Did they not see that God, who created them, is greater than them in strength?﴾ [Fussilat: 15]. And here He said: ﴿The likes of which were not created in the lands﴾, meaning: the tribe the likes of which were not created in their lands, because of their strength, might, and great physical make-up.

Mujahid said: Iram is an ancient nation, meaning the first ʿĀd, as Qatadah ibn Di'amah and al-Suddi said. Al-Suddi said: Iram is the seat of the kingdom of ʿĀd. This is a good, sound, and strong opinion.

Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Kalbi said regarding His saying, ﴿of the pillars﴾: they were people of a pillar, [i.e., of tent poles,] they did not settle in one place.

Al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: They were only called ﴿of the pillars﴾ because of their height.

Ibn Jarir chose the first opinion and rejected the second, and he was correct.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿The likes of which were not created in the lands﴾: Ibn Zayd took the pronoun to refer back to the pillars, because of their height, and he said: "They built pillars in al-Ahqaf, the likes of which were not created in the lands." As for Qatadah and Ibn Jarir, they took the pronoun to refer back to the tribe, meaning: the likes of that tribe were not created in the lands, that is, in their time. This view is the correct one. The view of Ibn Zayd and those who follow his approach is weak, because if he had meant that, it would have said: "The likes of which were not made in the lands," but He said: ﴿was not created the likes of which in the lands﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father told us, Abu Salih, the scribe of al-Layth, told us, Muʿawiyah ibn Salih told us, from one who narrated to him, from al-Miqdam, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he mentioned Iram of the pillars and said: "A man among them would come to a rock, lift it, and throw it upon the tribe, destroying them." [[This was also transmitted by Ibn Mardawayh in his Tafsir, as cited in Fath al-Bari by Ibn Hajar (8/701).]]

Then Ibn Abi Hatim said: ʿAli ibn al-Husayn told us, Abu al-Tahir told us, Anas ibn ʿIyad told us, from Thawr ibn Zayd al-Dili, who said: "I read a book, whose author he named when he read it: 'I am Shaddad ibn ʿĀd, and I am the one who raised the pillars, and I am the one who strengthened with my arm one glance, and I am the one who stored a treasure of seven cubits, which none will bring out except the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).'"

I say: According to every view, whether the pillars were buildings they constructed, or the poles of their tents for the desert nomads, or weapons with which they fought, or the height of each of them, they were a tribe and a nation among the nations. They are the ones mentioned in the Qur'an in more than one place, paired with Thamud, as they are here, and God knows best. As for whoever claims that the meaning of His saying, ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾, is a city, whether Damascus, as narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and ʿIkrimah, or Alexandria, as narrated from al-Qurazi [[in A: "al-Qurtubi".]], or something else, there is a problem with this, for how would the sentence fit with this: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd, Iram of the pillars?﴾ If it is taken as a substitution (badal) or as ʿatf al-bayan, the sentence does not hold together. Furthermore, the intended meaning is only to inform about the destruction of the tribe called ʿĀd, and what God brought upon them of His might which cannot be repelled, not to inform about a city or a region.

I have pointed this out so that one is not deceived by much of what a group of the exegetes mentioned at this verse, namely the mention of a city called ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾, built with bricks of gold and silver, whose palaces, houses, and gardens, whose pebbles are pearls and jewels, whose dust is musk pellets, whose rivers flow, whose fruits are abundant, whose houses have no inhabitant, whose walls and doors turn yellow, with no caller and no answerer in it, and which moves: at times it is in the land of Syria, at times in Yemen, at times in Iraq, and at times in other lands. All of this is from the fabrications of the Israelites, put forward by some of their heretics, to test with it the intellects of ignorant people, to see whether they will believe them in all of it.

Al-Tha'labi and others mentioned that a man from the Bedouins, who was ʿAbd Allah ibn Qilabah, in the time of Muʿawiyah, went in search of camels of his that had strayed. While he was wandering in searching for them, he came upon a great city with a wall and gates. He entered it and found in it something similar to what we have mentioned of the qualities of the golden city mentioned earlier. He returned and informed the people, and they went with him to the place he described, but they saw nothing.

Ibn Abi Hatim has mentioned the story of ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ here at great length, but this narration does not have a sound chain of transmission. Even if it were sound up to that Bedouin, he may have fabricated it, or some kind of madness and delusion afflicted him, so he believed that this had real existence outside the mind, when it does not. This is among matters whose unsoundness is certain. This is similar to what many ignorant, greedy, and deceptive people report, about the existence of treasures beneath the earth containing heaps of gold and silver, colors of jewels, rubies, pearls, and the great elixir, but there are barriers preventing access to them and taking from them. They then scheme against the wealth of the rich, the weak, and the foolish, consuming it wrongfully by spending it on incense, herbal remedies, and similar nonsense, and they mock them. What is certain is that the earth contains ancient treasures from the pre-Islamic and Islamic periods, and many hoards; whoever obtains some of them is able to transform them. But as for them being in the manner they claim, it is a lie, a fabrication, and a slander, and nothing of what they say is established except through their own transmission or the transmission of those who took from them. God, glory be to Him and exalted, is the Guide to what is right.

Ibn Jarir's statement: "It is possible that the meaning of His saying, ﴿Iram﴾, is a tribe or a town where ʿĀd used to dwell, and therefore it is not declined (lam tusraf)" has a problem with it, because the meaning from the context is only to inform about the tribe. For this reason He said after it: ﴿And Thamud, who carved out the rock in the valley﴾, meaning: they cut the rock in the valley. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they hewed it and cut through it. Likewise said Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd. From this one says "mujtabi al-nimar", meaning those who cut through the striped cloth, and ijtaba al-thawb means when he opened it. From it also comes the "jayb" (the opening of a garment). God, exalted, said: ﴿And you carve houses out of the mountains, skillfully﴾ [Al-Shuʿara': 149]. Here Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recited the verse of the poet:

Surely everything, except God, is perishing,
just as a tribe of Shanif and Marid perished.
They struck in every solid rock a hewing
with strong hands, sinewy of forearm.

[Tafsir al-Tabari (30/113).]

Ibn Ishaq said: They were Arabs, and their dwelling was in Wadi al-Qura. We have mentioned the story of ʿĀd in full in Surah Al-A'raf, sufficiently so that it need not be repeated.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿and Pharaoh, owner of the stakes﴾: al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: the stakes are the soldiers who strengthened his command. It is said that Pharaoh would fasten their hands and feet to stakes of iron, hanging them by them. Likewise Mujahid said: He used to fasten people to stakes. Thus said Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi. Al-Suddi said: He would tie a man, each of his limbs to a stake, and then send upon him a great boulder which would crush him.

Qatadah said: It has reached us that he had platforms and places of amusement, under which he would play, made of stakes and ropes.

Thabit al-Bunani said, from Abu Rafi': Pharaoh was called ﴿owner of the stakes﴾ because he drove four stakes for his wife, then placed upon her back a great millstone until she died.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿who transgressed in the lands and multiplied corruption therein﴾, meaning: they rebelled, became overbearing, and spread corruption in the earth through causing mischief and harm to people. ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a whip of punishment﴾, meaning: He sent down upon them a scourge from the sky and brought upon them a punishment that cannot be repelled from the criminal people.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: He hears and sees, meaning: He watches His creation in what they do, and recompenses each for his striving in this world and the Hereafter. All creatures will be presented before Him, and He will judge among them with His justice, and will deal with each according to what he deserves. He is free from injustice and oppression.

Ibn Abi Hatim has narrated here a very strange hadith, and its chain is questionable as to its soundness. He said: My father narrated to us, Ahmad ibn Abi al-Hawari narrated to us, Yunus al-Haddha' narrated to us, from Abu Hamza al-Baysani, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Mu'adh, verily the believer is a captive to the truth. O Mu'adh, verily the believer's fear does not subside and his agitation is not secure until he leaves the Bridge of Hell behind his back. O Mu'adh, verily the Qur'an restrains the believer from many of his desires, and from perishing in them, by the permission of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So the Qur'an is his guide, fear is his path, longing is his mount, prayer is his shelter, fasting is his shield, charity is his ransom, truthfulness is his commander, modesty is his minister, and his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is watching over all of that from behind [him]." [[Abu Nu'aym narrated it in al-Hilya (10/31) by way of Ishaq ibn Abi Hassan, from Ahmad ibn Abi al-Hawari with the same wording. Abu Nu'aym also narrated it in al-Hilya (1/26) by way of Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Karima, from Abu Hajib, from Abd al-Rahman, from Mu'adh, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) in similar wording.]].

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Yunus al-Haddha' and Abu Hamza are both unknown narrators (majhul, meaning their reliability is not established), and Abu Hamza's narration from Mu'adh is mursal (a break in the chain, where the Companion's name is missing). Had it been from Abu Hamza, it would have been good; that is, had it been from his own speech (not attributed to the Prophet), it would have been good.

Then Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Safwan ibn Salih narrated to us, al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, from Safwan ibn Amr, from Ayfa' ibn Abd al-Kula'i, that he heard him while he was admonishing the people, saying: "Verily Hell has seven bridges," and he said: "And the Sirat is over them." He said: "So the creatures will be held at the first bridge, and it will be said: ﴿And stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat: 24]. He said: They will be held accountable for the prayer and questioned about it. He said: Whoever is to perish, perishes there, and whoever is to be saved, is saved. When they reach the second bridge, they will be called to account for trust (amanah): how they fulfilled it and how they betrayed it. He said: Whoever is to perish, perishes, and whoever is to be saved, is saved. When they reach the third bridge, they will be questioned about the ties of kinship: how they upheld them and how they severed them. He said: Whoever is to perish, perishes, and whoever is to be saved, is saved. He said: On that Day the ties of kinship will be hanging down into the abyss of Hell, saying: O Allah, whoever has upheld me, then unite him, and whoever has severed me, then sever him. He said: And it is this of which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾."

Thus did he cite this report, but he did not mention its complete text.

**Tafsir of Surah al-Fajr**

It is a Meccan surah.

Al-Nasa'i said: Abd al-Wahhab ibn al-Hakam informed us, Yahya ibn Sa'id informed me, from Sulayman, from Muharib ibn Dithar and Abu Salih, from Jabir, who said: Mu'adh led a prayer, and a man came and prayed with him, and he [Mu'adh] prolonged it. So the man prayed in a corner of the mosque and then left. When this reached Mu'adh, he said: "He is a hypocrite." This was mentioned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he asked the young man. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I came to pray with him, and he prolonged it for me, so I left, prayed in a corner of the mosque, and tethered my water-camel." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Are you causing trouble, O Mu'adh? Where are you in relation to ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [87:1], ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [91:1], ﴿By the dawn﴾ [89:1], ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ [92:1]?" [Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra, no. 11673.]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

* *

As for ﴿al-Fajr﴾ (the dawn), it is well known, and it is the Subh (morning prayer/dawn). This was said by Ali, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah and al-Suddi. It is also reported from Masruq, Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b that what is meant is specifically the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr), which is the conclusion of the ten nights.

It was also said that what is meant is the prayer performed at that time, as Ikrimah said.

It was said that what is meant is the whole day. This is a report from Ibn Abbas.

As for ﴿the ten nights﴾: what is meant by them is the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, as said by Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and many others of the early and later scholars. It is established in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "There are no days in which righteous deeds are more beloved to Allah than these days" — meaning the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. They said: "Not even jihad in the way of Allah?" He said: "Not even jihad in the way of Allah, except for a man who goes out with his self and his wealth and does not return with anything of that." [Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 969.]

It was also said that what is meant is the first ten nights of Muharram. Abu Ja'far Ibn Jarir reported this without attributing it to anyone. Abu Kudayna narrated from Qabus ibn Abi Zibyan, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿and ten nights﴾, that he said: "It is the first ten [nights] of Ramadan."

The correct view is the first one. Imam Ahmad said:

Zayd ibn al-Hubab narrated to us, Ayyash ibn Uqba narrated to us, Khayr ibn Nu'aym narrated to me, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed the ten are the ten of al-Adha (Sacrifice), the odd is the Day of Arafah, and the even is the Day of Sacrifice."

al-Nasa'i narrated it from Muhammad ibn Rafi' and Abdah ibn Abd Allah, each of them from Zayd ibn al-Hubab, with the same chain. [al-Musnad (3/327) and Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra, no. 11671.] Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it from the hadith of Zayd ibn al-Hubab, with the same chain. [Tafsir al-Tabari (30/108).] This is a chain whose narrators are acceptable (la ba's bihim), but in my view the wording of its marfu' (traced-to-the-Prophet) form contains a strangeness (nakarah). And Allah knows best.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿By the even and the odd﴾: it has already been mentioned in this hadith that the odd is the Day of Arafah, because it is the ninth, and the even is the Day of Sacrifice, because it is the tenth. This was also said by Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah and al-Dahhak.

A second view: Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj narrated to us, Uqba ibn Khalid narrated to me, from Wasil ibn al-Sa'ib, who said: I asked Ata about His saying ﴿By the even and the odd﴾. I said: "Is it our prayer, this odd (witr) of ours?" He said: "No, but the even is the Day of Arafah, and the odd is the night of the Sacrifice."

A third view: Ibn Abi Hatim said: Muhammad ibn Amir ibn Ibrahim al-Asbahani narrated to us, my father narrated to me, from al-Nu'man, meaning Ibn Abd al-Salam, from Abu Sa'id ibn Awf, who narrated to me in Mecca, saying: I heard Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr giving a sermon to the people. A man stood up to him and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, inform me about the even and the odd." He said: "The even is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾, and the odd is His saying: ﴿and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾" [al-Baqarah 2:203].

Ibn Jurayj said: Muhammad ibn al-Murtafi' informed me that he heard Ibn al-Zubayr say: "The even is the middle of the days of Tashriq, and the odd is the last of the days of Tashriq."

In the two Sahihs, from the narration of Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one. Whoever enumerates them enters Paradise, and He is Odd (witr) and loves the odd." [Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 6410; Sahih Muslim, no. 2677.]

A fourth view: al-Hasan al-Basri and Zayd ibn Aslam said: All of creation is even and odd; Allah swore by His creation. This is also a report from Mujahid, but the well-known view from him is the first.

al-Awfi narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿By the even and the odd﴾ that he said: "Allah is one odd, and you are even." It is also said: the even is the dawn prayer (Subh) and the odd is the sunset prayer (Maghrib).

A fifth view: Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj narrated to us, Ubayd ibn Musa narrated to us, from Isra'il, from Abu Yahya, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿By the even and the odd﴾: "The even is the pair, and the odd is Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Abu Abd Allah said, from Mujahid: "Allah is the Odd, and His creation is the Even: the male and the female."

Ibn Abi Najih said, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿By the even and the odd﴾: "Everything Allah created is even: the heaven and the earth, the land and the sea, the jinn and the humans, the sun and the moon, and the like." Mujahid went in this direction with what they mentioned regarding the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And of everything We created pairs, that you may remember﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:49], meaning: so that you know that the Creator of the pairs is One.

A sixth view: Qatadah said, from al-Hasan: ﴿By the even and the odd﴾ is the number; within it is the even and within it is the odd.

A seventh view: concerning the noble verse, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir narrated it through the route of Ibn Jurayj. Then Ibn Jarir said: It has also been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) a report that supports the view we mentioned from Abu al-Zubayr: al-Husayn? [sic] Abd Allah ibn Abi Ziyad al-Qatawani narrated to me, Zayd ibn al-Hubab narrated to us, Ayyash ibn Uqba informed me, Khayr ibn Nu'aym narrated to me, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The even is the two days, and the odd is the third day." [Tafsir al-Tabari (30/109).]

This report has come in exactly this wording, and it contradicts what preceded in the wording of the narrations of Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Abi Hatim, and what he [Ibn Jarir] himself narrated. And Allah knows best.

Abu al-Aliyah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others said: It is the prayer. Among it is the even, like the four-rak'ah and two-rak'ah prayers, and among it is the odd, like the Maghrib, which is three, and it is the odd of the day. Likewise the Witr prayer at the end of the night's tahajjud.

Abd al-Razzaq said, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, from Imran ibn Husayn: ﴿By the even and the odd﴾: "It is the obligatory prayer; among it is the even and among it is the odd." This is disconnected (munqati') and halted (mawquf), and its wording is specific to the obligatory prayer. But it has been narrated connected and traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), with a general wording. Imam Ahmad said:

Abu Dawud, meaning al-Tayalisi, narrated to us, Hammam narrated to us, from Qatadah, from Imran ibn Isam: that a shaykh from the people of Basra narrated to him, from Imran ibn Husayn, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about the even and the odd, and he said: "It is the prayer; some of it is even and some of it is odd." [al-Musnad (4/437).]

This is how it appears in the Musnad. Likewise Ibn Jarir narrated it from Bundar, from Affan, and from Abu Kurayb, from Ubayd Allah ibn Musa, both of them from Hammam, meaning Ibn Yahya, from Qatadah, from Imran ibn Isam, from a shaykh, from Imran ibn Husayn. [Tafsir al-Tabari (30/109).] Likewise Abu Isa al-Tirmidhi narrated it from Amr ibn Ali, from Ibn Mahdi and Abu Dawud, both of them from Hammam, from Qatadah, from Imran ibn Isam, from a man from the people of Basra, from Imran ibn Husayn, with it. Then he said: "Gharib (strange); we do not know it except from the hadith of Qatadah, and Khalid ibn Qays also narrated it from Qatadah." [Sunan al-Tirmidhi, no. 3342.]

It has also been narrated from Imran ibn Isam, from Imran himself. And Allah knows best.

I say: Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it: Ahmad ibn Sinan al-Wasiti narrated to us, Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, Hammam informed us, from Qatadah, from Imran ibn Isam al-Dubaʿi, a shaykh from the people of Basra, from Imran ibn Husayn, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he mentioned it. Thus I saw it in his tafsir, where he made the Basran shaykh to be Imran ibn Isam [al-Dubaʿi].

Likewise Ibn Jarir narrated it: Nasr ibn Ali narrated to us, my father narrated to me, Khalid ibn Qays narrated to me, from Qatadah, from Imran ibn Isam, from Imran ibn Husayn, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding the even and the odd, that he said: "It is the prayer; among it is the even, and among it is the odd." [Tafsir al-Tabari (30/109).]

So he [the narrator] omitted the mention of the unnamed shaykh, and Imran ibn Isam al-Dubaʿi, Abu Umarah al-Basri, the imam of the mosque of Banu Dubay'ah, was alone in narrating it. He is the father of Abu Jamrah Nasr ibn Imran al-Dubaʿi. Qatadah narrated from him, and his son Abu Jamrah, al-Muthanna ibn Sa'id and Abu al-Tayyah Yazid ibn Humayd. Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat (the Reliable Narrators) [al-Thiqat (5/234)], and Khalifah ibn Khayyat mentioned him among the Successors (al-Tabi'in) from the people of Basra. He was a noble, honored man, highly regarded by al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf. Then he was killed on the day of al-Zawiyah in the year eighty-three (in another copy: eighty-two), because he went out with Ibn al-Ash'ath. He has in al-Tirmidhi only this single hadith. In my view, its being halted (mawquf) upon Imran ibn Husayn is more likely. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Jarir did not decide definitively on any of these views regarding the even and the odd.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾ [yasri]: al-Awfi narrated from Ibn Abbas: "That is, when it goes away."

Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr said: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾, until some of it removes the others.

Mujahid, Abu al-Aliyah, Qatadah, Malik, from Zayd ibn Aslam, and Ibn Zayd said: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾: "when it travels."

This can be understood according to what Ibn Abbas said, that is, it departs. It may also be that what is meant is when it travels, that is, it approaches. It may be said that this is more fitting, because it is in contrast to His saying ﴿and the dawn﴾, for the dawn is the approach of day and the withdrawal of night. So when His saying ﴿And the night when it passes﴾ is understood as its approach, it becomes an oath by the approach of night and the withdrawal of day, and vice versa, like His saying: ﴿And the night when it withdraws, and the morning when it breathes﴾ [al-Takwir 81:17–18]. Likewise al-Dahhak said: ﴿[And the night] when it passes﴾: that is, it flows.

Ikrimah said: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾ means: the night of Jam' (Muzdalifah). Narrated by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim.

Then Ibn Abi Hatim said: Ahmad ibn Isam narrated to us, Abu Amir narrated to us, Kathir ibn Abd Allah ibn Amr narrated to us, who said: I heard Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi say regarding His saying ﴿And the night when it passes﴾: "Pass on, O traveler, and do not reveal yourself except at Jam'."

* *

And His saying: ﴿Is there in that an oath for one of intellect?﴾ meaning: for one who has reason, understanding, and restraint [and religion] [[addition from manuscript M.]]. Reason is called ḥijr because it restrains a person from engaging in deeds and words that are unbecoming to him. From the same root comes ḥijr al-Bayt (the Hijr of the Ka'bah), because it prevents the circumambulator from pressing against its Syrian wall. Also from it is Ḥijr al-Yamamah (the Hijr of Yamamah). When a judge places a man under restriction (ḥajara 'ala fulan), he prevents him from disposing of his property. ﴿And they say, "A forbidding forbidding"﴾ [Al-Furqan: 22]. All of these belong to one category and have closely related meanings. This oath is by the times of worship and by worship itself, such as pilgrimage, prayer, and other kinds of acts of drawing near to God, by which His servants draw near to Him, the God-fearing who obey Him, who fear Him, who are humble before Him, and who are submissive to His noble Countenance.

When He mentioned these people, their worship, and their obedience, He said after them: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd?﴾ These people were rebellious, stubborn, and tyrannical, who departed from His obedience, denied His messengers, and rejected His scriptures. So God mentioned how He destroyed and annihilated them, and made them into tales and lessons. He said: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd, Iram of the pillars?﴾ These were the first ʿĀd, the descendants of ʿĀd ibn Iram ibn ʿAws ibn Sam ibn Nuh, as Ibn Ishaq said. They are the people among whom God sent His messenger Hud, peace be upon him, but they denied him and opposed him. So God saved him from among them, along with those who believed with him, and destroyed them with a violent, furious wind, ﴿which He imposed upon them for seven nights and eight days in succession, so that you would see the people in it fallen as if they were trunks of hollow palm trees. Do you see any remnant of them?﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 7–8]. God has mentioned their story in the Qur'an in more than one place, so that believers may take warning from their downfall.

So His saying, ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ [[in M: "bi-ʿĀd Iram".]] is ʿatf al-bayan (explicative apposition, ʿaṭf al-bayān, a noun placed after another to clarify it), serving to give further identification of them.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿of the pillars﴾: they used to live in tents of hair that were raised upon strong pillars. They were also the strongest people of their time in physical build and the most powerful in their force. For this reason Hud reminded them of that blessing and guided them to use it in obedience to their Lord who created them. He said: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Nuh and increased you in stature and build. So remember the bounties of God that you may succeed﴾ [[in M, A, H: "and do not commit corruption on earth, causing mischief," and the correct reading is what we have adopted.]] [Al-A'raf: 69]. And He said: ﴿As for ʿĀd, they were arrogant upon the earth without right and said, "Who is stronger than us in strength?" Did they not see that God, who created them, is greater than them in strength?﴾ [Fussilat: 15]. And here He said: ﴿The likes of which were not created in the lands﴾, meaning: the tribe the likes of which were not created in their lands, because of their strength, might, and great physical make-up.

Mujahid said: Iram is an ancient nation, meaning the first ʿĀd, as Qatadah ibn Di'amah and al-Suddi said. Al-Suddi said: Iram is the seat of the kingdom of ʿĀd. This is a good, sound, and strong opinion.

Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Kalbi said regarding His saying, ﴿of the pillars﴾: they were people of a pillar, [i.e., of tent poles,] they did not settle in one place.

Al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: They were only called ﴿of the pillars﴾ because of their height.

Ibn Jarir chose the first opinion and rejected the second, and he was correct.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿The likes of which were not created in the lands﴾: Ibn Zayd took the pronoun to refer back to the pillars, because of their height, and he said: "They built pillars in al-Ahqaf, the likes of which were not created in the lands." As for Qatadah and Ibn Jarir, they took the pronoun to refer back to the tribe, meaning: the likes of that tribe were not created in the lands, that is, in their time. This view is the correct one. The view of Ibn Zayd and those who follow his approach is weak, because if he had meant that, it would have said: "The likes of which were not made in the lands," but He said: ﴿was not created the likes of which in the lands﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father told us, Abu Salih, the scribe of al-Layth, told us, Muʿawiyah ibn Salih told us, from one who narrated to him, from al-Miqdam, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he mentioned Iram of the pillars and said: "A man among them would come to a rock, lift it, and throw it upon the tribe, destroying them." [[This was also transmitted by Ibn Mardawayh in his Tafsir, as cited in Fath al-Bari by Ibn Hajar (8/701).]]

Then Ibn Abi Hatim said: ʿAli ibn al-Husayn told us, Abu al-Tahir told us, Anas ibn ʿIyad told us, from Thawr ibn Zayd al-Dili, who said: "I read a book, whose author he named when he read it: 'I am Shaddad ibn ʿĀd, and I am the one who raised the pillars, and I am the one who strengthened with my arm one glance, and I am the one who stored a treasure of seven cubits, which none will bring out except the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).'"

I say: According to every view, whether the pillars were buildings they constructed, or the poles of their tents for the desert nomads, or weapons with which they fought, or the height of each of them, they were a tribe and a nation among the nations. They are the ones mentioned in the Qur'an in more than one place, paired with Thamud, as they are here, and God knows best. As for whoever claims that the meaning of His saying, ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾, is a city, whether Damascus, as narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and ʿIkrimah, or Alexandria, as narrated from al-Qurazi [[in A: "al-Qurtubi".]], or something else, there is a problem with this, for how would the sentence fit with this: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd, Iram of the pillars?﴾ If it is taken as a substitution (badal) or as ʿatf al-bayan, the sentence does not hold together. Furthermore, the intended meaning is only to inform about the destruction of the tribe called ʿĀd, and what God brought upon them of His might which cannot be repelled, not to inform about a city or a region.

I have pointed this out so that one is not deceived by much of what a group of the exegetes mentioned at this verse, namely the mention of a city called ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾, built with bricks of gold and silver, whose palaces, houses, and gardens, whose pebbles are pearls and jewels, whose dust is musk pellets, whose rivers flow, whose fruits are abundant, whose houses have no inhabitant, whose walls and doors turn yellow, with no caller and no answerer in it, and which moves: at times it is in the land of Syria, at times in Yemen, at times in Iraq, and at times in other lands. All of this is from the fabrications of the Israelites, put forward by some of their heretics, to test with it the intellects of ignorant people, to see whether they will believe them in all of it.

Al-Tha'labi and others mentioned that a man from the Bedouins, who was ʿAbd Allah ibn Qilabah, in the time of Muʿawiyah, went in search of camels of his that had strayed. While he was wandering in searching for them, he came upon a great city with a wall and gates. He entered it and found in it something similar to what we have mentioned of the qualities of the golden city mentioned earlier. He returned and informed the people, and they went with him to the place he described, but they saw nothing.

Ibn Abi Hatim has mentioned the story of ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ here at great length, but this narration does not have a sound chain of transmission. Even if it were sound up to that Bedouin, he may have fabricated it, or some kind of madness and delusion afflicted him, so he believed that this had real existence outside the mind, when it does not. This is among matters whose unsoundness is certain. This is similar to what many ignorant, greedy, and deceptive people report, about the existence of treasures beneath the earth containing heaps of gold and silver, colors of jewels, rubies, pearls, and the great elixir, but there are barriers preventing access to them and taking from them. They then scheme against the wealth of the rich, the weak, and the foolish, consuming it wrongfully by spending it on incense, herbal remedies, and similar nonsense, and they mock them. What is certain is that the earth contains ancient treasures from the pre-Islamic and Islamic periods, and many hoards; whoever obtains some of them is able to transform them. But as for them being in the manner they claim, it is a lie, a fabrication, and a slander, and nothing of what they say is established except through their own transmission or the transmission of those who took from them. God, glory be to Him and exalted, is the Guide to what is right.

Ibn Jarir's statement: "It is possible that the meaning of His saying, ﴿Iram﴾, is a tribe or a town where ʿĀd used to dwell, and therefore it is not declined (lam tusraf)" has a problem with it, because the meaning from the context is only to inform about the tribe. For this reason He said after it: ﴿And Thamud, who carved out the rock in the valley﴾, meaning: they cut the rock in the valley. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they hewed it and cut through it. Likewise said Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd. From this one says "mujtabi al-nimar", meaning those who cut through the striped cloth, and ijtaba al-thawb means when he opened it. From it also comes the "jayb" (the opening of a garment). God, exalted, said: ﴿And you carve houses out of the mountains, skillfully﴾ [Al-Shuʿara': 149]. Here Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recited the verse of the poet:

Surely everything, except God, is perishing,
just as a tribe of Shanif and Marid perished.
They struck in every solid rock a hewing
with strong hands, sinewy of forearm.

[Tafsir al-Tabari (30/113).]

Ibn Ishaq said: They were Arabs, and their dwelling was in Wadi al-Qura. We have mentioned the story of ʿĀd in full in Surah Al-A'raf, sufficiently so that it need not be repeated.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿and Pharaoh, owner of the stakes﴾: al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: the stakes are the soldiers who strengthened his command. It is said that Pharaoh would fasten their hands and feet to stakes of iron, hanging them by them. Likewise Mujahid said: He used to fasten people to stakes. Thus said Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi. Al-Suddi said: He would tie a man, each of his limbs to a stake, and then send upon him a great boulder which would crush him.

Qatadah said: It has reached us that he had platforms and places of amusement, under which he would play, made of stakes and ropes.

Thabit al-Bunani said, from Abu Rafi': Pharaoh was called ﴿owner of the stakes﴾ because he drove four stakes for his wife, then placed upon her back a great millstone until she died.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿who transgressed in the lands and multiplied corruption therein﴾, meaning: they rebelled, became overbearing, and spread corruption in the earth through causing mischief and harm to people. ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a whip of punishment﴾, meaning: He sent down upon them a scourge from the sky and brought upon them a punishment that cannot be repelled from the criminal people.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: He hears and sees, meaning: He watches His creation in what they do, and recompenses each for his striving in this world and the Hereafter. All creatures will be presented before Him, and He will judge among them with His justice, and will deal with each according to what he deserves. He is free from injustice and oppression.

Ibn Abi Hatim has narrated here a very strange hadith, and its chain is questionable as to its soundness. He said: My father narrated to us, Ahmad ibn Abi al-Hawari narrated to us, Yunus al-Haddha' narrated to us, from Abu Hamza al-Baysani, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Mu'adh, verily the believer is a captive to the truth. O Mu'adh, verily the believer's fear does not subside and his agitation is not secure until he leaves the Bridge of Hell behind his back. O Mu'adh, verily the Qur'an restrains the believer from many of his desires, and from perishing in them, by the permission of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So the Qur'an is his guide, fear is his path, longing is his mount, prayer is his shelter, fasting is his shield, charity is his ransom, truthfulness is his commander, modesty is his minister, and his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is watching over all of that from behind [him]." [[Abu Nu'aym narrated it in al-Hilya (10/31) by way of Ishaq ibn Abi Hassan, from Ahmad ibn Abi al-Hawari with the same wording. Abu Nu'aym also narrated it in al-Hilya (1/26) by way of Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Karima, from Abu Hajib, from Abd al-Rahman, from Mu'adh, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) in similar wording.]].

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Yunus al-Haddha' and Abu Hamza are both unknown narrators (majhul, meaning their reliability is not established), and Abu Hamza's narration from Mu'adh is mursal (a break in the chain, where the Companion's name is missing). Had it been from Abu Hamza, it would have been good; that is, had it been from his own speech (not attributed to the Prophet), it would have been good.

Then Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Safwan ibn Salih narrated to us, al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, from Safwan ibn Amr, from Ayfa' ibn Abd al-Kula'i, that he heard him while he was admonishing the people, saying: "Verily Hell has seven bridges," and he said: "And the Sirat is over them." He said: "So the creatures will be held at the first bridge, and it will be said: ﴿And stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat: 24]. He said: They will be held accountable for the prayer and questioned about it. He said: Whoever is to perish, perishes there, and whoever is to be saved, is saved. When they reach the second bridge, they will be called to account for trust (amanah): how they fulfilled it and how they betrayed it. He said: Whoever is to perish, perishes, and whoever is to be saved, is saved. When they reach the third bridge, they will be questioned about the ties of kinship: how they upheld them and how they severed them. He said: Whoever is to perish, perishes, and whoever is to be saved, is saved. He said: On that Day the ties of kinship will be hanging down into the abyss of Hell, saying: O Allah, whoever has upheld me, then unite him, and whoever has severed me, then sever him. He said: And it is this of which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾."

Thus did he cite this report, but he did not mention its complete text.

The Most High says, rebuking man for his belief when Allah expands provision for him in order to test him. He thinks that this is Allah's honouring him, but it is not so; rather, it is a trial and a test. As Allah the Most High said: ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children is us hastening to them with good? Nay, they do not perceive﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:55-56]. Likewise, on the other side, when He tries and tests him by restricting his provision, he thinks that this is Allah's humiliating him. Allah says: ﴿Nay﴾, meaning the matter is not as he claims, neither in this nor in that. Allah gives wealth to whom He loves and to whom He does not love, and He restricts it for whom He loves and for whom He does not love. The criterion in this is obedience to Allah in both states: if he is rich, by thanking Allah for it; and if he is poor, by being patient.

* *

His saying: ﴿Nay, you do not honour the orphan﴾ contains a command to honour him, as came in the hadith narrated by Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, from Sa'id ibn Abi Ayyub, from Yahya ibn Sulayman, from Zayd ibn Abi Attab [[In manuscript M: "Ghiyath".]], from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ: "The best house among the Muslims is a house in which there is an orphan who is treated well, and the worst house among the Muslims is a house in which there is an orphan who is mistreated." Then he said, pointing with his finger: "I and the guardian of the orphan will be in Paradise like this." [[Al-Zuhd of Ibn al-Mubarak, no. (654). It was also narrated by Ibn Majah in al-Sunan, no. (3679), by way of Ibn al-Mubarak. Al-Busiri said in al-Zawa'id (3/165): "This isnad is weak; Yahya ibn Sulayman (Abu Salih) — al-Bukhari said of him: munkar (rejected), and Abu Hatim said: mudtarib al-hadith (inconsistent in narration), but Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat."]]

Abu Dawud said: Muhammad ibn al-Sabbah ibn Sufyan narrated to us, ʿAbd al-ʿAziz (meaning Ibn Abi Hazim) informed us, my father narrated to me, from Sahl (meaning Ibn Sa'd), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I and the guardian of the orphan are like these two in Paradise," and he joined his two fingers: the middle finger and the one next to the thumb. [[Sunan Abi Dawud, no. (5150). It is also in Sahih al-Bukhari, no. (6005), by way of Ibn Abi Hazim with the same chain.]]

﴿Nor do you urge one another to feed the poor﴾ means: they do not command kindness to the poor and needy, nor do they encourage one another to do so. ﴿And you devour inheritance﴾ means: the inheritance ﴿greedily﴾, meaning from whatever source it came to them, whether lawful or unlawful. ﴿And you love wealth with immense love﴾, meaning abundant. Some of them added: excessively.

* *

* *

His saying: ﴿And Hell is brought forward on that Day﴾. Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj said in his Sahih: Umar ibn Hafs ibn Ghiyath narrated to us, my father narrated to us, from al-'Ala' ibn Khalid al-Kahili, from Shaqiq, from 'Abdullah – that is Ibn Mas'ud – who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hell will be brought on that Day, having seventy thousand bridles, with each bridle seventy thousand angels dragging it."

Likewise al-Tirmidhi narrated it from 'Abdullah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Darimi, from Umar ibn Hafs, with the same chain. He also narrated it from Abd ibn Humayd, from Abu 'Amir, from Sufyan al-Thawri, from al-'Ala' ibn Khalid, from Shaqiq ibn Salama – who is Abu Wa'il – from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, as his own statement, and he did not raise it to the Prophet. * *

His saying: ﴿On that Day man will remember﴾ meaning: his deeds and what he had sent forward in the far and recent past of his life. ﴿But how will remembrance benefit him?﴾ meaning: how will remembrance profit him? ﴿He will say: "Oh, would that I had sent forth for my life"﴾ meaning: he will regret what he had committed of sins, if he was a disobedient one, and will wish he had increased in acts of obedience, if he was an obedient one. As Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal said:

Ali ibn Ishaq narrated to us, 'Abdullah – meaning Ibn al-Mubarak – narrated to us, Thawr ibn Yazid narrated to us, from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayra – and he was one of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) – who said: "If a servant prostrated on his face from the day he was born until he died of old age in obedience to Allah, he would still regard it as insignificant on the Day of Resurrection, and he would wish that he were returned to the world so that he might increase in reward and merit."

Bahir ibn Sa'd also narrated it from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, from 'Utba ibn 'Abd, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). [Musnad (4/185).]

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So on that Day none will punish as He punishes﴾ meaning: there is no one whose punishment is more severe than the punishment of Allah for one who disobeyed Him. ﴿And none will bind as He binds﴾ meaning: and there is no one more severe in seizing and binding than the Zabaniyah (guardian angels of Hell) toward those who disbelieved in their Lord, Mighty and Majestic. This applies to the criminals among the creatures and the wrongdoers. As for the pure, tranquil soul, which is the calm, steadfast one that remains with the truth, it will be said to it: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord﴾ meaning: to His nearness, His reward, and what He has prepared for His servants in His Garden, ﴿well-pleased﴾ meaning: within itself, ﴿and pleasing﴾ meaning: it has been pleased with Allah, and Allah is pleased with it and has made it content. ﴿Enter among My servants﴾ meaning: among their number. ﴿And enter My Garden.﴾ This is said to it at the time of death, and also on the Day of Resurrection, just as the angels give good tidings to the believer at his death and when he rises from his grave, and likewise here.

Then the commentators differed as to who this verse was revealed about. Ad-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed about 'Uthman ibn 'Affan. And from Buraydah ibn al-Husayb: it was revealed about Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with him.

Al-'Awfi said, from Ibn 'Abbas: On the Day of Resurrection it will be said to the tranquil souls: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord﴾, meaning: your companion, which is its body that it used to inhabit in the world, ﴿well-pleased and pleasing﴾.

It is also reported from him that he used to recite it: "Enter among My servant and enter My Garden." Likewise Ikrimah and al-Kalbi said, and Ibn Jarir preferred it, but it is rare, and the first view is apparent, due to His saying: ﴿Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾ [al-An'am: 62] and ﴿And that our return is to Allah﴾ [Ghafir: 43], meaning: to His judgment and standing before Him.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Ali ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, Ahmad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abdullah al-Dashtaki narrated to us, my father narrated to us, from his father, from Ash'ath, from Ja'far, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing﴾, he said: It was revealed while Abu Bakr was sitting, and he said: "O Messenger of Allah, how beautiful this is!" He said: "Indeed, it will be said to you this." [Also narrated by Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya al-Maqdisi in al-Mukhtara, as in al-Durr al-Manthur (8/513).]

Then he said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj narrated to us, Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Ash'ath, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: I recited before the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing﴾, and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Indeed this is good." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Indeed the angel will say this to you at death."

Likewise Ibn Jarir narrated it from Abu Kurayb, from Ibn Yaman, with the same. This is a fine mursal report. [Tafsir al-Tabari (30/122); also narrated by Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, as in al-Durr al-Manthur (8/513).]

Then Ibn Abi Hatim said: al-Hasan ibn 'Arafa narrated to us, Marwan ibn Shuja al-Jazari narrated to us, from Salim al-Aftas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: Ibn 'Abbas died at al-Ta'if, and a bird came that was not seen in its form, and it entered his bier, then it was not seen coming out of it. When he was buried, this verse was recited at the edge of the grave, though it was not known who recited it: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing, so enter among My servants and enter My Garden.﴾

Al-Tabarani narrated it from Abdullah ibn Ahmad, from his father, from Marwan ibn Shuja, from Salim ibn 'Ajlan al-Aftas, with it, and mentioned it. [al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (10/290); al-Haythami said in al-Majma' (9/285): "Its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih."]

Al-Hafiz Muhammad ibn al-Mundhir al-Harawi, known as Shakkar, mentioned in his book "al-'Aja'ib," with his chain, from Qubath ibn Razin Abu Hashim, who said: I was taken captive in the lands of the Romans, and the king gathered us and presented his religion to us, on the condition that whoever refused would have his neck struck. Three of them apostatized, and a fourth came and refused, so his neck was struck, and his head was thrown into a river there. It sank in the water, then floated on the surface of the water, and it looked at those three and said: "O so-and-so, and O so-and-so, and O so-and-so," calling them by their names. Allah, exalted is He, says in His Book: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing, so enter among My servants and enter My Garden.﴾ Then it dove into the water, [he said,] and the Christians nearly became Muslim, the king's throne fell, and those three returned to Islam. He said: The ransom came from the Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur, and we were freed.

Al-Hafiz Ibn 'Asakir narrated in the biography of Rawaha bint Abi 'Amr al-Awza'i, from her father: Sulayman ibn Habib al-Muharibi narrated to me, Abu Umama narrated to me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to a man: "Say: O Allah, I ask You for a soul that is tranquil in You, that believes in meeting You, is content with Your decree, and is satisfied with Your bestowal." [Tarikh Dimashq (p. 100), "Tarajim al-Nisa"; al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (8/118) through 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd al-Ghaffar, from Rawaha bint 'Abd al-Rahman, with it.]

Then he narrated from Abu Sulayman ibn Zabr that he said: This hadith of Rawaha is one of its kind.

End of the commentary on Surah al-Fajr, and all praise is due to Allah [and His favor].
